title: The twelve links
hook: ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the senses, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, aging-and-death (SN 12.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: paticcasamuppada, dependent arising. When this is, that comes to be. Your line: leans on conditions.

Near the entrance of a Tibetan temple, you may find a huge painted wheel held in the claws and teeth of a fierce figure. Around its outer rim run twelve small pictures. A blind person with a stick. A potter at his wheel. A monkey swinging through a tree. People in a boat. A house with windows. A couple embracing. A man with an arrow in his eye. Someone drinking. Someone picking fruit. A pregnant woman. A birth. An old body being carried away. It looks like a puzzle. It's a teaching.
screen: `A PAINTED WHEEL BY THE DOOR.` → `TWELVE SMALL PICTURES.` → `A PUZZLE THAT'S A TEACHING.`

segments.voice: The very first sutta in the book on dependent arising, in the Connected Discourses, lays the chain out. With ignorance as condition, there are formations. Then the links run on: consciousness; name-and-form, the mind and body together; the six senses; contact, where a sense meets its object; feeling, pleasant, painful or neither; craving; clinging; becoming; birth; and finally aging and death, with sorrow, grief and despair. Such, the sutta says, is the arising of this whole mass of dukkha. Now match them to the wheel. Ignorance is the blind person, feeling the way. Formations, the potter, the way past actions shape what comes. Consciousness, the monkey jumping from branch to branch. Name-and-form, the people in the boat, traveling together. The six senses, the house with its windows. Contact, the embrace. Feeling, the arrow in the eye. Craving is drinking, clinging is grabbing fruit, becoming is the pregnancy, then birth, then the body carried off. The paintings are a later Indian and Tibetan tradition; the suttas give only the list. The same sutta then runs the chain again as an ending: with the ending of ignorance, formations end, and so on, link by link, to the ending of this whole mass of dukkha. Buddhists read the chain in more than one way. The Theravada commentaries spread it across three lifetimes: past, present and future. Some teachers also read it moment by moment, in a single afternoon. Both readings are part of the living tradition.
screen: `WITH IGNORANCE AS CONDITION.` · `TWELVE LINKS, ONE BY ONE.` · `THE BLIND ONE, THE POTTER, THE MONKEY.` · `ACROSS LIVES, OR IN A MOMENT.` · then, large: `TWELVE LINKS.`

segments.voice: On each breath, name one link and let its picture appear: ignorance, the blind one; formations, the potter; consciousness, the monkey; name-and-form, the boat; six senses, the house; contact, the embrace; feeling, the arrow; craving, drinking; clinging, grabbing fruit; becoming, the pregnancy; birth; aging and death. Then go around again, slower. If you lose your place, start at the blind one.
Nidana. A link in the chain of dependent arising: from ignorance to aging and death, each one leaning on the one before, and each one able to end.
Your line: twelve links. A puzzle on a temple wall, and a teaching. That's day three hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: In Tibetan monasteries the wheel of life is often painted near the entrance with the twelve links around its rim; in Theravada lands the links are chanted and studied, often following the commentaries' three-life reading.

fork.setup: you're looking at the wheel of life. you spot a monkey swinging from branch to branch. which link is it?
fork.reveal: the monkey is consciousness, jumping from one object to the next; craving is someone drinking, clinging is grabbing fruit.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit nidāna: a cause or source, the usual word for each of the twelve links.

trapdoor: what you thought: the twelve links are a list to memorize.
what it means: they show how dukkha arises one condition at a time, and how it ends the same way.

what a scholar hears: SN 12.1 opens the Nidānasaṃyutta with both the arising and the cessation sequence; Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga XVII sets out the three-life reading, while other teachers apply the links to a single moment.

chat.says: What's that painted wheel with twelve little pictures in Tibetan temples?
options: The twelve links of dependent arising, from ignorance to aging and death.
It's a calendar showing the twelve months and their festivals.
It shows twelve heavens a good person climbs through after death.
chat.meaning: The pictures on the wheel's rim show the twelve links of SN 12.1, from ignorance, the blind one, to aging and death.

Nidana.meaning: a link in the chain; a cause or source

dukkha.meaning: suffering, unease, the pain that comes with life

Theravada.meaning: the teaching of the elders, the school of the Pali canon

sources.ref: SN 12.1 (Paticcasamuppada Sutta), the twelve links forward and in reverse
Visuddhimagga XVII (dependent origination across three lives)

notes: Wheel-of-life iconography varies between paintings; confirm the standard Tibetan images (e.g. contact sometimes a couple embracing, becoming sometimes a pregnant woman or a couple, birth a woman giving birth, aging-and-death a corpse carried). The script hedges with 'a later Indian and Tibetan tradition'.
The wheel's origin is traced to a Vinaya account and Indian murals (e.g. Ajanta); 'later Indian and Tibetan tradition' should be confirmed.
Confirm that the moment-to-moment reading is fairly described as part of the living tradition (it has Abhidhamma precedents and modern advocates).
